The Message was transmitted to the Legislature on the 18th ultimo. It is (says the Bee) a document of considerable length, the importance of the occasion of which induces that journal to give the following extended analysis of it:

Gov. QUIRMAS declares that he calls the Legislature together first in obedience to certain joint resolutions which passed the General Assembly last year and next from and considerations which he proceeds to make known. This he does at extreme length. He holds that the contest between the North and the South, beginning in rival interests has assumed the character of hatred and bitterness, and is easily produced by incongruous and dissimilar social systems. Hostility to slavery he asserts is the controlling element of political action and party movement both in Congress and throughout the Northern States. As evidence of this he refers to California, and declares that the North formed a deliberate scheme to exclude the South from that region; that the transient population of California excited the sovereignty of the country and to cut off the South from all participation therein that the project was VIGOROUSLY and that its advocates were compelled to unite it with others which they termed compromise and that thus many patriotic members were deluded into its support.

The Legislature of Mississippi had declared that the South was entitled to an equal participation in the benefits derived from the territory acquired from Mexico and the Nashville Convention had indicated the line of 49 as the ultimatum of Southern concession. This position, the Gov thinks, would have commanded but for the want of firmness and unanimity in the South. OBJECTIONS occurred among her representatives, and the compromise bills were passed after nine months of anxious discussion. The sage contends that by the adjustment the South has been wronged, despoiled, and defrauded, and is especially wroth against the Texas bill which declares it has converted millions of slave territory into free.

The Message dwells largely upon the admission of California, contending that slavery should have been allowed to establish itself in that State, that slave labor would have been highly probable, that slaves would have worked the mines, remunerated their masters handsomely and greatly augmented their value. It likewise assumes the unique position that the admission of California is a violation of the constitution and attempts to draw a refined and unintelligible distinction between the admission of a Territory as a State and the admission of a State as a State; every State did pass through a probationary territorial period before being received by the Congress with the attributes of sovereignty, Governor QUIRMAS will have it. He too asserts that because the State of California excludes slavery, Congress has sanctioned the Wilmot Proviso. Against such folly is it folly to argue. The abolition of the slave trade in the District of Columbia, and municipal regulation, similar to enactments formerly in force in Mississippi and Maryland, likewise provokes the Gubernatorial ire.

The message thinks that nothing is to be hoped from the North, and that respite from aggression cannot be expected, that if slavery is left to the tender mercies of the Federal Government its fate is doomed. Here is his proposition in his own words:

"The Government of the United States is hostile to slavery. It will hereafter be selected with reference to its hostility to this interest, and its activity the doing of injury. If this great and vital interest remains subject to the government and control of its enemy, it must perish! Sooner or later, it must perish. To save it, to preserve it from destruction, at least from a sickly lingering, dismembered and precarious existence, it must be protected by guarantees more available than the present situation furnishes; it must be wrested from the control of the power which is hostile to it, and which seeks its destruction; it must, like every other great interest, be placed in charge of its friends."

After much in this style, the Governor proceeds to the question: What is to be done? Acquiescence, with the declaration that further aggression will be tolerated, he regards as base and cowardly. The crisis must be looked in the face. Mississippi must not submit. The remedy advised by Governor QUIRMAS is a State Convention, with full and ample powers to take into consideration federal relations, the aggressions committed upon the South, the dangers that threaten its domestic institutions and all kindred subjects, and jointly with other states, separately adopt such measures as may best comport with the dignity and safety of the State and equally correct the evils complained of. What exactly the Convention is to do does not appear, the Governor expressing his confidence in the wisdom of the people, and his full belief that they will steadily and firmly defend their rights. He suggests, however, as his views for a last effort at Cancellation, the proposition should be distinctly made to the people of the non-slaveholding States to remedy the wrong, for it may be in the power of Congress TO do so BY obtaining from California concessions south of 36° 30' and to pass such amendments of the Federal Constitution as shall hereafter amply the rights of the slaveholding States from misconception and further aggression. In the event of such concessions being obtained, he hesitates to recommend "PEACEABLE SECESSION." In other words, the Governor DESTROYS that Congress should abandon the safe and impregnable principle of non-intervention and resort to legislation on the subject of slavery, with the clear conclusion staring him in the face that if the power be conceded to the Federal Government to prohibit slavery above 36° 30', the entire authority necessarily granted will restrict that institution to any other latitude hereafter. Such a dangerous grant of power will be spurned by the sovereigns of the South, spurned less than two years ago by JOHN C. CALHOUN and every Southern statesman, Gen. QUIRMAS himself included. And in default of the acceptance of such a weapon to pierce the heart of the South, the Governor of Mississippi holds that the State should secede. Monstrous conclusion to a most fallacious and sophistical argument!

Having devoted nine-tenths of his message to distorted and partial consideration of the slavery question, Governor QUIRMAS in closing addresses slightly on matters of local interest.

A LARGE FAMILY--A CHALLENGE TO KENTUCKY.

We had the pleasure of being present on Monday
last, at a family gathering in the town of Guilford
which exceeded all that we have ever seen even at
a New England Thanksgiving. The patriarch of
this numerous race was MR. James Davis, a soldier
of the revolution, now eighty-five years old. His
wife, who is past eighty, retains the vivacity and
cheerfulness of middle age, and on this occasion
moved among her descendants with the sprightli-
ness of one of her grandchildren. There were
present at the tea-table children, seven chil-
dren-in-law, thirty grandchildren, ten grand
children-in-law, and eleven great-grandchildren
in all, sixty-six.

children-in-law, and eighteen great-grandchil-

ninety-nine living members of the family. Besides
these, thirteen have died, making the whole num-
ber on the family record one hundred and twelve.

of one pair. But the most honorable fact in this
patriarchal household remains to be recorded:
There is not an old maid or a bachelor among
them! Not only is every child married, but every
grandchild who has reached the age of twenty-six
years. Is there anything in Kentucky that can
beat this?—New Haven Journal.

The Senate having under consideration the resolutions


Mr. HOUSTON arose and addressed the Senate as follows.


Mr. PRESIDENT: However incompetent I may be to repay the Senate for their courtesy permitting to address them at this time, and upon this subject, I feel that it is my duty to offer my respectful, frank, and candid MANNER as representative of that State whose interests are involved in the resolutions offered for consideration by the distinguished senator from Kentucky Mr. CLAY, and in his connexion, I trust it may not be considered out of place for me to make a resolution which offered some days since. It is not said expressly to instruct how this assembly is bent upon. While other gentlemen, more distinguished, more able and more enlightened upon all subjects than myself, casting into the treasury of knowledge their abundance, may be allowed to cast in my small contribution, I can only assure you, Mr. President, that no one feels a more sincere desire than myself that the present agitation of this country cease, and the violent emotions which have influenced the deliberations of the Congress of the United States put to rest. All that I regret is that my ability is too inadequate to the accomplishment, of which I vainly trust that shall not be without gentlemen of influence in this chamber to step forward and advocate this Union, the harmony of these States, and the happiness of us all. It is a subject of importance, and one in which all others are involved.


These considerations awaken my solicitude for the adoption of the resolution which I had the honor few days since to submit. The Senate cannot be expected that the country will enjoy either happiness or prosperity, while we see practical suspension of that congressional action which is necessary to the maintenance of general prosperity, or until Congress again, in good earnest, fulfills the duties which devolved upon it by virtue of its Representative character. I trust, Mr. President, that it may not be inappropriate to request the reading of the resolution submitted by me.

Resolved, That the people in the Territories have the inherent right of the people in the newly acquired Territories, by the annexation of the South of the parallel of 36 deg. and 30 min. of latitude, extending to the Pacific, shall establish or prohibit such establishment of negro slavery in the formation of their own governments, and that such prohibition shall be no objection to the admission of such State into the Union of the United States."


Mr. HOUSTON resumed. Mr. President, my object in the introduction of this resolution is to present a ground which I believed was equitable and just between the conflicting interests and prejudices of this country. I believe in the first place, that the Congress of the United States has no power over the subject of slavery, either within the Territories or any other section of the Union. This averment is contained in the resolution which I have presented, and whatever the decision of this body may be with reference to the subject, I have great reason to defer to the opinions of gentlemen superior to myself in knowledge and experience; nevertheless, in my humble way, I have the right to interpose my opinion where the interests of the country, and every individual within the Confederacy, are vitally and materially affected. It is equally my duty to express here such sentiments as I entertain upon a subject which involves, as I consider, not only my interests and the interests of my constituents, but the dearest interests of every citizen of the United States. For sir, if the constitution is disregarded, the power of the nation is admitted to belong to Congress—beyond the letter of the constitution, where it is not indispensable to the existence of the nation, to maintain it is an act of usurpation, and ought not to be exercised.


The North contend that they have a right to interfere with the subject of slavery: hence the Wilmot Proviso. The South contend that the North has no such right—no right to interfere with the subject of slavery anywhere, and hence the principle is contended for, that Congress does not possess this power applicable to the Territories—no power arising from the terms of the UNION between the North and the South, none growing out of the constitution by which they are bound together. Nor do I believe that Congress has, under the constitution, any authority to impose upon States asking for admission into the Union any condition whatever, other than that of having a republican form of government. A State in order to be admitted into this Union, except that its constitution shall be republican, and that the imposition of any other by Congress would only be in violation of the constitution, but in direct conflict with the principle on which our political system rests."

We have examples of the adoption of this policy, for example, the admission of Texas into this Confederacy of States. some numbers of the Freeman, copy of which
I ordered to this place some two years SINCE.

last four or five weeks, and not being aware

the qualification to myself as well as for that of
others, and the good of the cause, I request
you to continue sending the Freeman to Hun-

slavery friends, I trust we have not been un-
profitably employed, if in no other way than in
storing our minds with useful information and
in forming acquaintance with men and things
as they really exist in the great West. We
have seen too, some of the workings of the
"peculiar institution." Passing through Mary-
land, we more than once had the modification
of being waited on by slaves and were very
politely and kindly entertained by their masters.
So far from lessening our adherence to the
evil, however, as appears to be the case with
some, it had directly the contrary effect. As
an instance of the effect of slavery upon men
who under other circumstances, perhaps,

tion, really do appear to be kind, and benevo-
lent, and honorable men, will relate the fol-

the hotels.


A long table was spread in the dining room,
several well dressed and no doubt well fed
slaves were waiting upon it; the landlord, aside
from his slaveholding, appeared to be a gentle-
man. Most of the stage passengers had eaten
their suppers; one had no money to pay for
his; and the landlord was hunting him up to give
him his supper; he allowed no one to go from
his house hungry. "God only knows what may
of us may come to it." A tall gentleman from
the South responded heartily to the generous
and humane sentiments of the landlord,
"I like the way a man talks, sir," he said; and then, changing the subject,
he inquired as it was uncertain whether he was in
Maryland or in old Pennsylvania, "what State

After a pause, "Are niggers selling, sir?"
"Are there any selling here!" "No, sir, there
are none selling just now." "I bought a very
fine woman for my own use for three hundred
francs," was the answer.

of slavery after such an exhibition as this. I
was about to give expression to some thoughts
that followed the above development in rela-
tion to the magnitude, the length, breadth, and
depth of the evil which we are endeavoring to
eradicate, but I fear they will readily sing
themselves. How I would like to introduce the
Freeman into a thousand families in
this western world, but that is out of the ques-
tion. The Bugle is sent by a friend unknown
into the neighborhood, and very worthy and
pious people think it very wrong to take it
from the post Office. What an incalculable
amount of prejudice and ignorance we have to
encounter. The people are all opposed to sla-
very, and yet an anti-slavery paper is a per-
nicious publication. The people do not under-
stand the question, and I suppose we shall have
to keep on trying to make them understand it.

A NEW Daily Paper to be published in Washington City, D. C.
THE UNDERSIGNED will shortly publish at the seat of the National Government daily the United States.

The elements of national revolution, evolved from the passions of mankind, always tend to fatal examinations; but it is the prerogative of an enlightened public will to control them, and make them subservient to wise and patriotic issues. Such elements are now fearfully at work in the United States, tending avowedly to a revolution which every patriot would deplore as the greatest calamity that could possibly befall this country. The efforts of the Union Party alone avert that calamity—the united efforts of those who, nobly relinquishing personal and old party considerations, are determined to stand shoulder to shoulder for "liberty and the Union, now and forever, one and inseparable."

The fires of American patriotism require to be rekindled in the hearts of too many of our countrymen. Evil influences from abroad have found their way amongst them, and smothered the flames which ought never to subside in American bosoms. In one section of the country an ignis fatuus has been held up as light to better prosperity in another, the moral sentiment has been stimulated to monomania, with the design of effecting collision between the North and the South and dissolution of the American Union. Even now, the missionaries of ruin, scenting blood from afar, are hovering, like vultures, in the hope of a conflict.

It is high time, therefore, for patriotic Americans, for men of both the old parties—to throw aside their old traumas and divisions, and to unite in one greater party for the salvation of the country. It is high time that they should wake from their false security, and look their real danger in the face; to reassert their true American character and resolve with energy never to be relaxed that no foreign or domestic foe shall stay the course of their country's glorious destiny.

It will be the earnest purpose of "THE CONSTITUTION" faithfully to represent the sentiments of the Union party. It will recognise no Whig or Democrat; but every one friend or foe to the Union, the Constitution, and the laws; and it will advocate those measures and only those which the Union party will sanction. With these principles and motives, "THE CONSTITUTION" will take the field "thrice armed in the cause of our common country—fully confident of success, and of the liberal support of enlightened and still independent people.

The first number will be published as soon as the necessary mechanical arrangements shall be completed.
